newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FEATURE-Pachyderm pill proves a jumbo job.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Pachyderm pill proves a jumbo job.

text.p: Animal scientists are trying to perfect an elephant birth control method, but they face major problems including the prospect of thousands of sex-mad tuskers rampaging through the bush.

Although most countries in Africa are more concerned with a decline in elephant numbers because of ivory poaching, some, like South Africa, have to cull the animals because they breed too fast for the available space.

Many animal welfare groups are bitterly opposed to culling, calling it cruel and unnecessary, but the South African National Parks Board says it has few alternatives in its quest to maintain bio-diversity.
Since 1967 it has killed about 400 elephants a year in the Kruger National Park to keep the population there stable at around 7,500, the maximum it believes the game reserve can accommodate.
The parks board believes that if elephants were allowed to breed unchecked, they would destroy habitat needed by other animals and would become a danger to communities on the park boundaries.
The board also transfers elephants from the Kruger Park to other smaller game reserves but these are also rapidly reaching capacity.
Contraception could be the answer, and this month the board sanctioned an independent experiment with a potential birth control method for jumbos known as porcine zona pellucida (PZP).
Developed in the United States, the pig-derived chemical should effectively immunise elephants against pregnancy by preventing sperm from fertilising the adult elephant cow's eggs.
A pilot group of 21 elephant cows have been implanted with slow-release capsules containing the chemical and they will receive a booster dose a month later.

Rudi van Aarde, professor of zoology at the University of Pretoria, said it could take four and a half years to discover if the method worked because this was the average calving interval in elephants.
"Testing PZP depends on conducting the experiment on live animals but it needs to be a controlled and limited number of elephants," he said in an interview.
"We don't know yet if immunisation will destroy the ovary."

Van Aarde said German researchers were trying to develop an elephant contraceptive based on the hormone oestrogen while he and his colleagues at the University of Pretoria were working on a third method that would prevent the uterus from preparing itself for conception.
"With all three methods, we may disturb the individual elephant to such an extent that none is practical," he said.
"With the hormone treatment for example, the animal may want to have to sex all the time and the hormone might even induce cancerous growths," he said.

Van Aarde said he and a zoologist from the University of Tennessee had formulated a model of the elephant population in the Kruger National Park that predicted that to maintain zero population growth, 76 percent of all adult cows would have to be on contraception.
"It's a formidable task. Can you imagine 76 percent of elephant cows in the park, that's 3,000 animals, feeling very sexy all the time? It would be chaos."
He said the direct costs of such a programme, excluding labour, would be 2.7 million rand ($600,000) a year.

"Why bother to pursue it, you might ask. Our motivation is that we as scientists are paid by the taxpayer, and many taxpayers are negatively affected by culling. It's my duty as a scientist to find an alternative to culling."
Van Aarde said he had begun researching elephant reproduction in 1990 and the work had proved far more complex than expected.
"The hormones controlling pregnancy in elephants are different to those in any other mammal... We're a long way from getting answers," he said.
